source_text: Tintinnabula et mala granata in ora vestis — sonus doctrinae et fructus operum. Ingrediens sancta audiatur.
thought_title: Bells and pomegranates on the priestly robe
orientation: Origen is interpreting the high priest's vestments from Exodus, applying each item to the moral and doctrinal life of the Christian teacher.
pass_a_gloss: Bells and pomegranates on [the] hem [of] [the] garment — [the] sound [of] teaching and [the] fruit [of] works. [The] holy [woman] entering let [her] be heard.

choices.why: The literal object on the priestly robe; the glossary does not cover it, so the plain English word is used.
The literal fruit named in the source; kept as the concrete object Origen allegorizes.
Ora means the edge or border of a garment; 'hem' is the standard English term for the garment's edge.
Sonus is the literal sound made by the bells; doctrina is teaching, matching Origen's allegory of the priest's voice.
Fructus is fruit, operum is works; the pomegranates symbolize the tangible results of good deeds.

choices.english: When he enters the holy place, let him be heard
choices.why: Ingrediens is a present participle with temporal force; sancta is neuter plural accusative of place; audiatur is a jussive subjunctive, preserving the command force.
rejected: Entering the holy things, he is heard
As he enters the sanctuary, he should be heard

bible_refs.note: Tintinnabula et mala granata in ora vestis

pass_b_english: Bells and pomegranates along the hem of the garment: the sound of teaching and the fruit of works. When he enters the holy place, let him be heard.

last_rejected.why: Latin is passive 'let him be heard/audible'; English keeps passive but 'let him be heard' implies permission, not 'he should be heard/audible'.
last_rejected.fix: When he enters the holy place, he must be heard.
last_rejected.ruling: Passive subjunctive 'audiatur' naturally renders as 'let him be heard'; jussive sense is standard and not misleading.
